extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in mathematics and the history/process of mathematical proof
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-magazine feature recounting Andrew Wiles' attempts to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, focusing on how proofs are checked, how gaps are found and repaired, and the peer-review process in mathematics. It draws lessons about what makes a mathematical proof acceptable or fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must be checked and verified before acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a proof is proposed, it must be checked and verified before it is accepted as valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes how Wiles submitted a 200-page proof which was divided among six reviewers; reviewers scrutinized every logical step and requested clarifications from Wiles. Acceptance depends on peer verification and satisfaction of reviewers' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical completeness — no gaps in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical argument must not contain gaps; a gap (a faulty anchor point) can undermine the entire proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Katz and Illusie found lines of reasoning they couldn't follow; what began as a seemingly minor oversight turned into a critical gap. Gaps may sometimes be repaired with small fixes or require new techniques; unrepairable gaps can render a proof invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every logical step must be followable by peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be able to follow and verify each logical step in a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewers encountered a line they couldn't follow, they questioned it and contacted Wiles. Authors must provide explanations or fixes for any steps that peers cannot verify. Clear exposition and detailed justification for steps are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use and verification of prior results/assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs must rely on established results only when those results truly apply; tacit or incorrect assumptions can invalidate a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites historical examples (Cauchy and Lamé assuming unique factorization for complex numbers) where incorrect tacit assumptions led to false proofs; Kummer introduced ideals to address the issue. Authors must ensure that used theorems/assumptions are valid in context or provide necessary new tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process and division of expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals divide long manuscripts among multiple expert reviewers who scrutinize assigned sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles' manuscript was divided among six reviewers; specialized reviewers (e.g., Katz) examined particular sections in detail. The editorial process facilitates deep scrutiny by experts in subareas and allows iterative corrections via correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and seeking outside expertise to repair gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author encounters a serious gap, collaborating with other experts or seeking alternate approaches is an accepted method for repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles recruited Richard Taylor and consulted others; they tried localized fixes, then broadened their search for approaches and ultimately used Iwasawa theory together to mend the gap within weeks. Collaboration can bring new perspectives and techniques to resolve problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative or later-developed methods may be necessary and acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to employ advanced or newly developed mathematical tools to complete a proof, provided they are valid and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles ultimately used Iwasawa theory and other modern instruments—ideas invented long after Fermat—to complete the proof. The article emphasizes that using later-developed methods is legitimate, though it means the final proof is unlikely to be Fermat's original demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and conceptual correctness of mathematical structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical claims depend on correct handling of definitions and structures (e.g., unique factorization), and failures here can cause incorrect proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative about Kummer and the failure of unique factorization in certain complex integers illustrates how deep structural issues can invalidate purported proofs; resolving such problems may require inventing new concepts (ideals) or reworking foundational assumptions.
